newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Unocal says Afghan pipeline worth wait.
newsitem.headline: Unocal says Afghan pipeline worth wait.

text.p: The Afghan war is blocking a $2 billion gas pipeline project, but Unocal Corp. is willing to wait for years to build it in peace, a Unocal executive said.

"If the war continues, the pipeline won't happen," Marty Miller, Unocal vice president for new ventures in Central Asia and Middle East, said in Islamabad, discussing the planned Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan pipeline.

"We are willing to stay two of three years at the minimum," said Miller, whose company is to be the leader in an international consortium to develop the pipeline, which will link Turmenistan's vast natural gas reserves with the growing Pakistani and Indian markets.

Pakistan and Turkmenistan have demonstrated inter-government support for the project through various agreements, and Unocal said leaders of all major factions in Afghanistan, including the dominant Taleban Islamic movement, have also signed project support agreements or letters.

However, Miller said the final terms of an arrangement for the passage of the pipeline through Afghanistan against payment of a transit fee could be negotiated only with a stable and internationally recognised government.
He would not say when work on the project could be started because of various complex agreements involved and the uncertaintly of the situation in Afghanistan.
But he said: "Once we get all the agreements in place, we can probably build this thing and have it finished in two to three years."

The 48-inch pipeline is planned to extend 910 miles from the Daulatabad gas field in southeastern Turkmenistan to the southern Pakistani city of Multan, with approximately 465 miles of it crossing through Afghanistan.
A future 400-mile extension to a terminus near the Indian capital, New Delhi, is also possible. Miller said the proposal had received support both in Pakistan and India, which are archrivals.
He said there was no consensus in Pakistan about extending the pipeline to India, but most of the people with whom he discussed the matter had supported the idea.

"I would say in general, there is a support for the idea because we believe it's win-win," he said. "By having higher volumes going through the pipelines onto India, because of the economy of scale, it would reduce the cost of the gas in Pakistan."
The extension will also be good for India because "the Indians in the New Delhi area are desparately short of energy," he said.
The Unocal-led consortium will include Saudi Arabia's Delta oil compauy, the Turkmen government, Russia's Gazprom gas company and one more company each from Pakistan and Japan.
Miller said the project's economic fundamentals were "strong enough that we are willing to risk a considerable sum of money."

But he added: "And when I say risk, it's all dependent to large extent on when there is peace in Afghanistan and when there is a government we can work with. It may be next year, may be the end of this year, may be three years."
